summaries.summary: Stance detection, also called stance identification or stance classification, is a recent NLP classification problem outputting {Favor, Against, Neither} for a text and target pair.
Stance detection is usually considered a sentiment analysis subtask, differs by targeting a particular target, and can support information retrieval and other text analysis systems.

Previous stance detection work includes sentiment and arguing features, dialogue structure, machine learning experiments, topic-independent disagreement features, student essays, and Wikipedia-based controversial topic stances.

Recent related work includes unseen target stance detection, SCIFNET, a crowdsourced stance and sentiment tweet data set with six predefined targets, and SemEval 2016 Twitter Stance Detection with 19 systems.
This paper presents a publicly available Turkish tweet data set stance-annotated for two popular football clubs and evaluates SVM classifiers using unigram, bigram, and hashtag features.
The authors claim this is the first study targeting stance detection in Turkish tweets and hope its data set and SVM baselines increase Turkish social media analysis studies.
The paper is organized into sections describing the annotated tweet data set, SVM-based stance classifiers and evaluations, future research topics, and a concluding summary.
The authors chose tweets about popular sports clubs, with Galatasaray as Target-1 and Fenerbahçe as Target-2, to facilitate using football followers' opinions.
The authors used one Turkish data set of 1 million random tweets from August 18 to September 6, 2015, filtered by club names, and annotated Favor or Against stances.
The authors did not annotate tweets with the Neither class and treated the club as the stance target even when management or a particular footballer was discussed.
The annotation process produced 700 balanced tweets, with 175 Favor and 175 Against tweets for each target, and publicly available CSV stance annotations with three columns.
The authors claim this is the first publicly-available stance-annotated data set for Turkish and the first stance-annotated data set including sports-related tweets.
The authors trained two SVM classifiers, one for each target, using unigrams as features on the 700-tweet data set after automated stopword filtering.
The authors used Weka's SVM implementation with the SMO algorithm and a linear kernel, reporting 10-fold cross-validation results using precision, recall, and F-Measure.
Evaluation results are favorable, especially for Target-1 and the Favor class, and are compared with BIBREF0 baselines and SVM-based sentiment analysis systems.
SVM classifiers using only bigrams performed poorly, leading the authors to conclude that unigram-based features are superior on their data set.
The authors added the existence of hashtags in tweets as an additional feature to unigrams and provided SVM evaluation results in Table TABREF2.
Compared with Table TABREF1, Table TABREF2 shows a 0.5% F-Measure decrease for Target-1 and a 1.8% overall F-Measure increase for Target-2.
The authors state their evaluation results are significant reference results and support unigram-based and hashtag-related features in SVM classifiers for Turkish tweet stance detection.

The paper concludes by presenting a publicly available Turkish stance-annotated tweet data set for two popular sports clubs and SVM classifiers with 10-fold cross validation reference results.
